newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Russian troops to prepare for Tajik refugee influx.
newsitem.headline: Russian troops to prepare for Tajik refugee influx.

text.p: The chief of Russia's border guards said on Tuesday his troops in Tajikistan must prepare for the return of thousands of refugees and fighters to the former Soviet republic from neighbouring Afghanistan.

"It's necessary today to create the conditions for the return of refugees and fighters of the United (Tajik) Opposition," General Andrei Nikolayev told reporters at the start of a two-day visit to Tajikistan, which has been shattered by four years of civil war.

In agreement with the Tajik government, Russia deploys some 20,000 soldiers in the Central Asian state. They guard the remote, mountainous frontier with Afghanistan and China and perform peacekeeping duties, viewing themselves as a bulwark against militant Islam.

But Nikolayev was in Tajikistan to review Russian military commitments in the light of a peace agreement signed last month between the republic's secular government and armed Islamic rebels, the United Tajik Opposition.
A spokesman for Russia's Federal Border Service in Dushanbe said earlier that Nikolayev would broach the possibility of a 10 percent cut in Russian forces along the Tajik-Afghan frontier.

But after meeting Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov, Nikolayev said that while the situation on the border had "changed radically", it would be several months before any troop reductions would be considered.
"When the situation allows we will ourselves decide on a reduced force capable of protecting the state border," he said.
A potential flashpoint is the return of guerrillas to the republic from Afghanistan.

"Armed people must not cross the border," Nikolayev said. He did not give further details but this is unlikely to go down well with the fighters, many of whom doubt the safety guarantees promised under the June accord.
Russian soldiers have had regular skirmishes with opposition guerrillas who operated out of bases across the border in Afghanistan.
In June, Russian border guards said they killed about 30 fighters when they tried to cross the border east of Dushanbe. The incident rocked a delicate ceasefire agreed last December.
The war killed tens of thousands in the republic of 5.7 million while many more fled their homes, some to dust-blown refugee camps over the border in Afghanistan.
Nikolayev said he had also been commanded by Russian President Boris Yeltsin and Tajikistan's Rakhmonov to step up the fight against drugs trafficking along the border.

Russian soldiers regularly clash with smugglers who cross the treacherous waters of the Pyandzh River in inflatable dinghies to smuggle in opium destined for markets in western Europe from Afghanistan.
"In connection with this group (smugglers), we must tighten security along the state border," Nikolayev said.
The border guards also form a thin green line between Russia and its former Central Asian colonies on one side and Afghanistan's purist Islamic Taleban militia on the other.
The advances of black-turbaned Taleban troops have rattled the nerves of the region's ex-Soviet republics who fear Afghan-style instability could spill over their borders.
